.
We define the
c
-fanout from
q\in Q
over a word
v
as the set of
paths from
q
over
v
that start by assigning 1 to
c
(by
\Delta^{\mathit{in}}_{x}
or

\Delta^{1}_{x}
) and go on by copying or incrementing
c
(by
\Delta^{\mathit{inner}}_{x}
or
\Delta^{+}_{x}
) only.

Lemma 2

Let
\pi
be a path in the
c
-fanout from
q

split by transitions from
\Delta^{+}_{x}
into
n+1
fragments,
n\in\mathbb{N}
(new fragments start with the transition from
\Delta^{+}_{x}
). Then, assuming
c=\overline{S}\texttt{\lx@text@lbrace}m,n\texttt{\lx@text@rbrace}
, each fragment reads a word in
L(S)
or is a prefix of some word for the last fragment.
Furthermore,
\pi
increments
c

n
-times and each fragment except the first one starts in some state from
\text{last}({c})
.

Appendix 0.C
Complexity of Computing and Simulating
\mathtt{DCSA}^{\mathtt{a}}(R)

Let
R
be a regex with flat counting
and let
A=\mathtt{CA}(R)=(X,Q,\Delta,I,F)
.
If
X
is non-empty (and in further we assume it is), then for a state
(R,\mathit{Act})
of
\mathtt{DCSA}^{\mathtt{a}}(A)
, the set of states
R
is unnecessary, it is possible to obtain it from the set of active counters
\mathit{Act}
(as every
x_{r}
,
r\in R
must have some value, i.e. some
x_{S}
with
r
or
r^{\texttt{+}}
in
S
must be active).
Each state of
\mathtt{DCSA}^{\mathtt{a}}(A)
is then uniquely represented by some subset of
X^{\mathtt{a}}=X\times\mathcal{P}(Q\cup Q^{\texttt{+}})
, i.e.
\mathtt{DCSA}^{\mathtt{a}}(A)
has
O(2^{|X|2^{|Q|}})
states. However, because
R
has flat counting, for each
q\in Q
there is at most one
x\in X
such that
x_{q}
can have non-zero value in
A
. Therefore, there will be at most
O(2^{2^{|Q|}})
states in
\mathtt{DCSA}^{\mathtt{a}}(A)
.

For each state
(R,\mathit{Act})
there are at most
O(2^{|\Delta|})=O(2^{|Q|^{2}})
transitions starting from it (
|\Delta|
has at most
|Q|^{2}
transitions for regexes with flat counting, see
Lemma

1
), as we create transition for each minterm of
\mathtt{DCSA}(A)
which are conjunctions of guards of transitions from
A
.
Furthermore, the size of each transition depends on the size of its guard and the size of the update function.
The size of the guard (i.e. minterm) of transitions in
\mathtt{DCSA}(A)
is
O(|Q|)
as each such guard is conjunction of predicates
x_{q}<\max_{x}
and
x_{q}\geq\min_{x}
, for each
q\in Q
with its at most one nonzero counter
x\in X
, and their negations.
As we replace each
x_{q}
in this guard by disjunction of
x_{S}
,
q\in S
, for
\mathtt{DCSA}^{\mathtt{a}}(A)
, the size of the guard in
\mathtt{DCSA}^{\mathtt{a}}(A)
is
O(|Q|2^{|Q|})
.
As each
x_{S}
can occur only in one term in the update (we cannot have counter replication), its size is
O(|X|2^{|Q|})
, however, with similar reasoning as for number of states, the size of the update can be reduced to
O(2^{|Q|})
.
The size of
\mathtt{DCSA}^{\mathtt{a}}(A)
is then
O(2^{2^{|Q|}}*2^{|Q|^{2}}*|Q|2^{|Q|})=O(|Q|2^{2^{|Q|}})

Lemma 3

The size of
\mathtt{DCSA}^{\mathtt{a}}(A)
is in
O(|Q|2^{2^{|Q|}})
.

From the construction of
(\mathtt{DCSA}^{\mathtt{a}}(A)
and the described encoding of configurations of
\mathtt{DCSA}(A)
by those of
\mathtt{DCSA}^{\mathtt{a}}(\mathtt{CA}(R))
, it follows that

L(\mathtt{DCSA}^{\mathtt{a}}(\mathtt{CA}(R)))=L(\mathtt{DCSA}(\mathtt{CA}(R)))
.
Furthermore, for
R
with flat counting,
\mathtt{CA}(R)
is Cartesian, thus we get:

Lemma 4

L(\mathtt{CA}(R))=L(\mathtt{DCSA}^{\mathtt{a}}(\mathtt{CA}(R)))
.

Section

5
gives worst-case time approximations for membership check with automata with non-replicating counters.
We now reduce these approximations for
\mathtt{DCSA}^{\mathtt{a}}(A)
.
To find the next CSA transition from state
(R,\mathit{Act})
to be taken with a set interpretation
\mathfrak{s}
and symbol
a
, we must traverse through all
a
-transitions starting in
(R,\mathit{Act})
whose guards are minterms.
We need to test each minterm, however we know that testing of atomic predicate is constant time operation, therefore finding the next CSA transition can be done in
O(|Q|2^{2|Q|})
as there are at most
O(2^{|Q|})
minterms whose size is at most
O(|Q|2^{|Q|})
(with similar reasoning as for the size of
\mathtt{DCSA}^{\mathtt{a}}(A)
).

The step that applies the update of selected transitions is amortized
O(|X^{\mathtt{a}}|)=O(|X|2^{|Q|})
, however, we can reduce this to
O(2^{|Q|})
for flat counting.
The cost of entire matching of a word
w
is then
O(|w|(|Q|2^{2|Q|}+2^{|Q|}))=O(|w||Q|2^{2|Q|})
.

Lemma 5

The cost of entire matching of a word
w
with
\mathtt{DCSA}^{\mathtt{a}}(A)
is in
O(|w||Q|2^{2|Q|})
.

Appendix 0.D
Proof of
Theorem

7.1

See
7.1

The theorem is shown using the two technical lemmas below
that capture a crucial relation between paths through
\mathtt{CA}(R)
and
\mathtt{DCSA}^{\mathtt{a}}(\mathtt{CA}(R))
.
We use here the notation from
Section

0.B.1
.

Lemma 6

Let there be a path of
\mathtt{CA}(R)
over a word
w
from its initial state to some state
q_{i}
and let
\pi_{1}
,
\pi_{2}
be two paths of
x
-fanout from the state
q
over a word
v
such that
\pi_{1}
increments
x

k+1
-times ending in the state
r
, and
\pi_{2}
increments
x

k
-times ending in the state
p
.
Then, if
\mathtt{DCSA}^{\mathtt{a}}(\mathtt{CA}(R))
exists, then there is a path over
wv
in
\mathtt{DCSA}^{\mathtt{a}}(\mathtt{CA}(R))
that ends with an active counter
x_{S}
such that
r^{\texttt{+}}\in S
and
p\in S
.

Proof

Assume that
\mathtt{DCSA}^{\mathtt{a}}(\mathtt{CA}(R))
exists.
As
\mathtt{DCSA}^{\mathtt{a}}(\mathtt{CA}(R))
is created using extension of classical subset construction, the path over
w
must lead to a state
(T,\mathit{Act})
s.t.
q\in T
.
Let
v=a_{1}\dots a_{n}
,
\pi_{1}[i]
(
\pi_{2}[i]
),
1\leq i\leq n
, be the path containing first
i
transition of
\pi_{1}
(
\pi_{2}
), and
r_{i}
(
p_{i}
) be the state in which of the path
\pi_{1}[i]
(
\pi_{2}[i]
) ends (i.e.
r_{i}=r
).
Furthermore, let
\pi
be the path from
(T,\mathit{Act})
over
v
in
\mathtt{DCSA}^{\mathtt{a}}(\mathtt{CA}(R))
and
(T_{i},\mathit{Act}_{i})
be the ending state of
\pi[i]
, for each
i
,
1\leq i\leq n
.
We now show that for each
i
,
1\leq i\leq n
, the numbers of increments of
x
occurring in
\pi_{1}[i]
and
\pi_{2}[i]
are either

•

same and there is
x_{S_{i}}\in\mathit{Act}_{i}
where
r_{i},p_{i}\in S_{i}
, or

•

differ by one. Here, if
\pi_{1}[i]
contains one more increment than
\pi_{2}[i]
, then there is
x_{S_{i}}\in\mathit{Act}_{i}
where
r_{i}^{\texttt{+}},p_{i}\in S_{i}
(similarly if
\pi_{2}[i]
contains one more increment).

We show this by induction on
i
.

For
i=1
,
because
\pi_{1}
and
\pi_{2}
are in
x
-fanout, their first transition from
q
to
r_{1}
and
p_{1}
must assign
1
to
x
.
Therefore, the counters will be shared during the construction, i.e. there is
x_{S_{1}}
to which we assign
1
in the first transition of
\pi
and
r_{1},p_{1}\in S_{1}
.

Let now assume the statement holds for
1\leq k<n
and we want to show that it also holds for
k+1
.
First, because
k+1>1
and
\pi_{1}
and
\pi_{2}
are in
x
-fanout, we have that the transitions at the end of
\pi_{1}[k+1]
and
\pi_{2}[k+1]
must either copy or increment
x
.
We now assume that the number of increments of
x
occurring in
\pi_{1}[k]
is one more than in
\pi_{2}[k]
(the case when they are the same has similar reasoning).
We know that there is
x_{S_{k}}\in\mathit{Act}_{k}
where
r_{k}^{\texttt{+}},p_{k}\in S_{k}
.
If the transitions at the end of
\pi_{1}[k+1]
and
\pi_{2}[k+1]
have the same operation for
x
, then the same operation (possibly with filter) is done at the end of
\pi[k+1]
for
x_{S_{k}}
and the statement hold for
k+1
(because the counters are still shared with the same increment postponing).
If the transition at the end of
\pi_{1}[k+1]
just copies
x
while the one at the end of
\pi_{2}[k+1]
increments it, then
x_{S_{k}}
is incremented at the end of
\pi[k+1]
(i.e. increments are synchronized), there is
x_{S_{i}}\in\mathit{Act}_{i}
where
r_{i},p_{i}\in S_{i}
, and
\pi_{1}[k+1]
and
\pi_{2}[k+1]
have the same number of increments.
Finally, the situation where the transition at the end of
\pi_{1}[k+1]
increments
x
while the one at the end of
\pi_{2}[k+1]
copies it cannot happen.
This is because the transition at the end of
\pi
would have to do two increments on
x_{S_{k}}
which is not allowed, i.e.
\mathtt{DCSA}^{\mathtt{a}}(\mathtt{CA}(R))
would not exist which is a contradiction.

,
1\leq i\leq n
, be the transitions of
\pi
.
Let
x_{S_{l}},x_{S_{l+1}},\dots,x_{S_{n}}
, for some
1\leq l\leq n
, be a sequence of counters where
{S_{n}}={S}
, for each
l<j\leq n
we have that term
u_{j}(x_{S_{j}})
contains
x_{S_{j-1}}
, and
u(x_{S_{l}})
does not contain any counter.
Intuitively, this is a sequence of names of the same counter that starts by mapping either 0 or 1 to
x_{S_{l}}
(and we will show it can actually be only 1) and then the values of this counter are further just copied or incremented to following counter until we end with
x_{S}
.
Furthermore,
l\not=n
, otherwise
u_{n}(x_{S})
would contain no counter and there would be no reason for
r^{\texttt{+}}
to be in
S
.
It also holds that each
S_{j}\subseteq Q_{x}
, as each
u_{j}(x_{S_{j}})
contains
x_{S_{j-1}}
and from the way the construction works, this means that there is a transition from each state of
S_{j-1}
to some state of
S_{j}
with
x
being copied or incremented, i.e. they are transitions from
\Delta^{\mathit{inner}}_{x}
or
\Delta^{+}_{x}
(which also means that
S_{l}\subseteq Q_{x}
).
We can also show that
S_{l}=\text{first}({x})
, because
u(x_{S_{l}})
does not contain any counter, i.e.
u(x_{S_{l}})=1
and this update is constructed from some transitions of
\Delta^{\mathit{in}}_{x}
or
\Delta^{1}_{x}

We now take
u=a_{1}\dots a_{l-1}
,
v=a_{l}\dots a_{n}
and the state
q
is some initial state of the transitions from
\Delta^{\mathit{in}}_{x}
or
\Delta^{1}_{x}
.
Obviously, there is a path of
\mathtt{CA}(R)
over
u
going to
q
and we can show by induction that for each
x_{S_{j}}
we have that:

•

if
q_{1},q_{2}\in S_{j}
, then there are paths
\pi_{1}
to
q_{1}
and
\pi_{2}
to
q_{2}
of
x
-fanout from the state
q
over a word
a_{l}\dots a_{j}
such that they both increment
x
same amount of times and

•

if
q_{1}^{\texttt{+}},q_{2}\in S_{j}
, then there are paths
\pi_{1}
to
q_{1}
and
\pi_{2}
to
q_{2}
of
x
-fanout from the state
q
over a word
a_{l}\dots a_{j}
such that
\pi_{1}
increments
x
one more time than
\pi_{2}
.

The proof of this is very similar to the proof used for
Lemma

6
.
Finally,
S
must contain some non-marked state
p
, otherwise it would not be possible to have
r^{\texttt{+}}
in
S
(
S
cannot contain only marked states, because otherwise increment would have been synchronized in
u_{n}(c_{S})
).

Proof
(Proof of
Theorem

7.1
)

(
\Rightarrow
)
By contradiction.
Assume that
\mathtt{CA}(R)
exists but
R
is does not have synchronizing counting, hence, it has a sub-expression
S\texttt{\lx@text@lbrace m,n\lx@text@rbrace}
which does not have synchronizing counting.
There exist words
u=u_{1},\ldots,u_{k}
and
v=v_{1},\ldots,v_{k+1}
that are a counterexample to
S\texttt{\lx@text@lbrace m,n\lx@text@rbrace}
having synchronizing counting, i.e.
v
is a prefix of
u
.
We assume w.l.o.g. that
k
is the smallest number with which such a counterexample can be obtained.
In
\mathtt{CA}(R)
, since it satisfies the conditions of
Section

0.B.1
, there is
a path
\pi
to a source
q_{i}
of an entry transition on the counting loop of
the counter
x
that is connected with the sub-expression
S\texttt{\lx@text@lbrace m,n\lx@text@rbrace}
.
Let
w
be the word of that path.
There must be two paths of
\mathtt{CA}(R)
in
x
-fanout from
q_{i}
over
v
.
One of them,
\pi_{1}
, ends by a transition to some state
q
in
\text{last}({x})
and it increments
x

k
-times (corresponding to processing
the word
v_{1}\cdots v_{k+1}
, by
Lemma

2
); the other one,
\pi_{2}
, corresponds to a prefix of
u_{1}\cdots u_{k}
. By
Lemma

2
we know it must increment
x
at most
k-1
times and if it incremented it fewer times, it would mean that we could remove some words
u_{l}\ldots u_{k}
,
l\leq k
, from
u
and
v
would still be a prefix of this word.
This would mean that we could have taken smaller
k
and we would be still able to find counterexample to synchronizing counting, but
k
is already smallest such one.
Therefore,
\pi_{2}
increments
x
exactly
k-1
times and we can now apply
Lemma

6
to find path of
\mathtt{DCSA}^{\mathtt{a}}(\mathtt{CA}(R))
over
wv
such that it ends in state
(T,\mathit{Act})
with some active counter
x_{S}\in\mathit{Act}
where
q^{\texttt{+}}\in S
.
However, because
q\in\text{last}({x})
, there is some transition
\delta
in
\mathtt{CA}(R)
that starts in the state
q
and has
x\mathbin{:=}x+1
in its update.
Now, during the construction of some transition from
(R,\mathit{Act})
that uses
\delta
we would get irresolvable counter replication and
\mathtt{DCSA}^{\mathtt{a}}(\mathtt{CA}(R))
would not exist, which is a contradiction.

(
\Leftarrow
) By contradiction. Assume that
R
has synchronizing counting, but
\mathtt{DCSA}^{\mathtt{a}}(\mathtt{CA}(R))
does not exist.
Take the shortest path
\pi
over some word
w
to some state
(T,\mathit{Act})
such that the construction of
\mathtt{DCSA}^{\mathtt{a}}(\mathtt{CA}(R))
failed while creating some transition from
(T,\mathit{Act})
.
This must mean that there is some
x_{S}\in\mathit{Act}
with some
q^{\texttt{+}}\in S
and
q\in\text{last}({x})
.
Let
S\texttt{\lx@text@lbrace m,n\lx@text@rbrace}
be the sub-expression of
R
whose counting loop in

\mathtt{CA}(R)
uses a counter
x
.
From
Lemma

7
we get two words
u,v
,
w=uv
and two paths
\pi_{1}
and
\pi_{2}
in some
x
-fanout of some
q_{i}
where
\pi_{1}
ends in
q
and increments
x

k+1
-times and
\pi_{2}
increments
x

k
-times.
From
Lemma

2
and
q\in\text{last}({x})
, we can divide
v
to
v_{1},\ldots,v_{k+2}
(corresponding to the path
\pi_{1}
) where
v_{i}\in L(S)
.
If we add to
\pi_{2}
some path over some word
v^{\prime}
so that it ends in some state from
\text{last}({x})
(without adding any transition that increment
x
), we can then divide
vv^{\prime}
to
u_{1}\ldots u_{k+1}
.
However,
v
is a prefix of
vv^{\prime}
, which means that we found words
v_{1},\ldots,v_{k+2}
and
u_{1}\ldots u_{k+1}
that show that
S\texttt{\lx@text@lbrace m,n\lx@text@rbrace}
does not have synchronizing counting, which is a contradiction.

Figure 3

The authors of
[

]
claimed that if regex
R
contains counting loops only of type

where
\alpha_{1}
denotes a set of symbols disjoint with any symbols from

,

, then the created CA can be determinized by their algorithm into CSA that accepts the same language.
However, for regex

, which satisfies the syntactic criterion, we get a counting automaton
A
on
Figure

3(a)
created by construction from
[
23
]
.
The determinized CSA
A^{\prime}
shown on
Figure

3(b)
is created according to the algorithm from
[
23
]
.
However, the word containing only

symbols
a
is accepted by
A^{\prime}
but not by
A
.

Appendix 0.F
Recognizing Letter Marked Counting

The following simple procedure determines whether a regex
R
has letter-marked counting. It inductively computes for a regex
R
the set
T_{R}
of all sets of marker-letters. We use
\Sigma(R)
as the set of all symbols occurring in
R
.

•

For
R=\texttt{a},a\in\Sigma
, we have
T_{R}=\{{\{{a}\}}\}
, as there is only one word
a\in L(R)
. For
R=\epsilon
, we have
T_{R}=\{\}
.

•

For
R=R_{1}\texttt{|}R_{2}
, we know that for each
T_{1}\in T_{R_{1}}
, each word in
L(R_{1})
contains exactly one symbol from
T_{1}
. However, there might be words in
L(R_{2})
that do not contain any symbol from
T_{1}
or they contain more than one symbol. If we are given some
T_{2}
from
T_{R_{2}}
, we can see that symbols from
\Sigma(R_{2})\setminus T_{2}
can occur more than once, or not occur at all, therefore, we can just test if
T_{1}\cap(\Sigma(R_{2})\setminus T_{2})=\emptyset
. We then take

T_{R}=\{\,T_{1}\cup T_{2}\,|\,T_{1}\in T_{R_{1}},T_{2}\in T_{R_{2}},T_{1}\cap(\Sigma(R_{2})\setminus T_{2})=\emptyset\text{ and }T_{2}\cap(\Sigma(R_{1})\setminus T_{1})=\emptyset\,\}.

•

For
R=R_{1}\,R_{2}
, we know that symbols from
T\in T_{R_{1}}
occur in words from
R_{1}\,R_{2}
exactly once, if they do not occur in the word given by
R_{2}
, i.e. if
T\cap\Sigma(R_{2})=\emptyset
. We can therefore take

T_{R}=\{\,T\,|\,T\in T_{R_{1}}\text{ and }T\cap\Sigma(R_{2})=\emptyset\,\}\cup\{\,T\,|\,T\in T_{R_{2}}\text{ and }T\cap\Sigma(R_{1})=\emptyset\,\}.

•

For
R=R^{\prime}\texttt{*}
, no set of marker-letters exists, as repeating words from
R^{\prime}
forces each letter to occur more than once. For this case,
T_{R}=\{\}
.
